beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali. This video is about measuring how private company share prices actually move, and how a new price spreads from one fund manager to the next. For seven weeks I was building a panel of prices out of S E C filings. This week I stopped building it and started measuring it. Five thousand four hundred and seventy-nine marks, four questions.

show.event: Cream Claude composer, empty. Serif greeting 'Szia, HAI' + terracotta spark above it.
The ask types itself into the composer, character by character.
Send button arms terracotta; running indicator reads 'measuring 5,479 marks…'.
Three output lines land in sequence — the ask arrives ANSWERED (COLD OPEN LAW).

props.segment: Measuring How Private Marks Move and Propagate
props.command: Stop building the marks panel and measure it. How often does a price actually change? Is that rate the same everywhere? Do two managers pricing the same company on the same date agree? And how fast does a new price level travel?
output: 25.0% of 4,079 steps unchanged — the plan expected 30–40%
and that headline hides everything: 0.0% to 48.5% by company
median same-date spread 10.8%; a new level reaches half its holders in 30 days

beats.narration_text: Four questions, and the panel answered all four against expectation. Prices move more often than the plan predicted. The headline rate hides almost everything. Managers pricing the same company on the same day usually hold different prices. And a new price level takes a median of thirty days to reach half the managers who will carry it.

shot.visual_intent: The BLUF as a question sheet: every row carries what was expected beside what was measured, so the reel's shape is visible in ten seconds.

show.event: The headline sets, then four question rows land in sequence.
Each row's measured answer resolves to its right, with the expectation beneath.
The measured population lands across the foot.

props.sparkLine: It stopped growing. It started answering.
props.headline: Four questions, four surprises.

questions.q: How often does a price change?
Is that rate the same everywhere?
questions.note: one number would have been true and useless

questions.q: Do two managers agree on a date?
How fast does a new level travel?
questions.note: 15 of 37 arrive on the same period end

props.popNote: marks — 5,479 less the 301 held out of every change series

beats.narration_text: First question. How often does a mark just get carried forward unchanged? The plan expected thirty to forty percent. Measured, it is twenty-five. And this is not an artifact of where I drew the line. I widened the test three ways, and even the most generous reading stays below the plan's band. Private marks move more than the plan assumed they would.

shot.visual_intent: Rebuild of pantry/w8-remark.png. The three widenings must be seen to CLIMB toward the band and stop short — that is what makes the result a disagreement rather than a threshold choice.

show.event: The plan's band draws as a grey span on a 0–50% axis.
The measured value lands as a terracotta mark, clearly outside and below the band.

show.at: on 'I widened the test three ways'
show.event: Three widened readings step up in sequence, each still short of the band.

show.at: on 'move more than the plan assumed'
show.event: The verdict lands across the foot.

props.title: Carried forward unchanged
props.subtitle: 4,079 consecutive observations, guarded
props.verdict: Even the most generous reading — anything under 1% counted as flat — is 29.6%, still under the band. The finding is not a threshold.

beats.narration_text: Second thing. That one number across the whole panel would have been true and useless. Split by company, the same statistic runs from zero for Groq to forty-eight percent for X dot A I. Anthropic and OpenAI are repriced at nearly every observation. X dot A I and SpaceX get carried forward a third to a half of the time. Same panel, same rule, completely different behaviour.

shot.visual_intent: Rebuild of pantry/w8-bycompany.png. The panel-wide rate is drawn as a RULE across the bars so its uselessness is visible — it passes near nothing.

show.event: Ten bars grow in rank order, each labelled with its share and its step count.
The top bar takes the accent.
The whole-panel rate draws as a single line across all ten bars, matching none of them.

props.title: The same statistic, by company
props.subtitle: share of consecutive observations carried forward unchanged
props.smallNote: Sample sizes span two orders of magnitude — 10 steps for Perplexity AI against 1,812 for Databricks. Each bar carries its own n, so 0.0% on 11 steps is not read as the same kind of fact as 19.8% on 1,812.
props.verdict: Same panel, same rule. The headline describes none of them.
props.source: SOURCE: figdata_week8.json — remark.by_company, sorted by share unchanged

beats.narration_text: Third question. When two managers price the same company on the same date, do they agree? Mostly not. Across a hundred and thirty same-date groups, the median spread between the highest and lowest price is just under eleven percent. Ninety-two of those groups hold more than one distinct price level. Different prices on the same date is the normal state here, not the exception.

shot.visual_intent: Rebuild of pantry/w8-dispersion.png. The highlight threshold is the measured p90 — it used to be hard-coded at 0.4 (README defect 3).

show.event: 130 dots fill a spread axis, one per group.
The median line drops through the field.
The multi-level groups light terracotta and the count resolves.
The p90 marker lands and the verdict follows.

props.title: 130 same-date groups
props.subtitle: spread between the highest and lowest price, one dot per group

counts.label: hold more than one price level

props.steadyNote: 38 groups sit on a single level with a median spread of 0.0% — the stack at zero. The other 92 hold more than one level and spread across the rest of the axis; only the ones past the dashed line are above the p90.
props.verdict: Different prices on the same date is the normal state, not the exception.
props.source: SOURCE: figdata_week8.json — same_date_stats.spreads; the highlight is the MEASURED p90, not a round number

beats.narration_text: That raises an objection. Maybe those gaps are just timing. A new round lands, and some managers have picked it up and others have not. So I opened one window. Anthropic preferred stock, two consecutive period ends, eight managers, eleven marks, running from a hundred and forty-one up to two hundred and sixty-two. You can see the old level, the new one, and managers crossing between them.

shot.visual_intent: Rebuild of pantry/w8-window.png. Both readings must be visible AT ONCE — this beat exists to stop B04 being over-read as 'managers disagree about value'.

show.at: on 'maybe those gaps are just timing'
show.event: The objection sets as the beat's premise.
Eleven dots land on a price axis, split into two period-end columns.
The lowest cluster bands in ink.
The largest cluster bands in terracotta.
The managers appearing in both columns are joined, and the in-between marks are named as mid-crossing.

props.sparkLine: A round arriving, one manager at a time.
props.title: One window, opened
props.subtitle: Anthropic preferred · 8 managers · 11 marks · 2025-12-31 → 2026-01-31
props.clusterNote: Levels are single-linkage at 2% relative gap — the same rule the findings module uses. The figure used to hard-code the split at a price threshold.
props.verdict: Not disagreement about value. A round arriving, one manager at a time.
props.source: SOURCE: figdata_week8.json — window[]; manager and mark counts are COUNTED, and the levels are clustered, not thresholded

beats.narration_text: Last question. I took every price level that three or more managers adopted, thirty-seven of them, and measured how long it took to reach half its holders. The median is thirty days. Fifteen of the thirty-seven get there on the very same period end. The slowest takes ninety-two days.

shot.visual_intent: Rebuild of pantry/w8-propagation.png. The 15 zero-day events must be visible as a stack AT zero — the distribution's shape is the finding, not the median alone.

show.event: 37 lag values land as a dot column on a 0–92 day axis.
The median line drops through them.

show.at: on 'on the very same period end'
show.event: The 15 zero-day events light terracotta at the axis origin.
The slowest event is marked at the far end.

props.title: How long a new level takes to reach half its holders
props.subtitle: 37 price levels adopted by 3 or more managers
props.zeroLabel: of 37 reach half on the SAME period end
props.toAllLabel: days, median, to reach ALL holders
props.toAllNote: First-to-last is the weaker number: it counts managers still carrying an old level long after the company repriced, which is staleness, not slow propagation. That is why the headline is first-to-half.

beats.narration_text: Two things that number is not. It cannot be shorter than the reporting calendar. A manager filing on the thirtieth of April cannot reflect a thirty-first of March repricing any sooner. So this measures observability, not diligence. And the figure originally claimed the biggest events travel fastest. I checked, and it does not hold.

shot.visual_intent: A claim the author made, checked, and removed — shown with the arithmetic that removed it, not just asserted as corrected.

show.at: on 'cannot be shorter than the reporting calendar'
show.event: The first bound lands with the 55-period-end, 5-distinct-days figure.
The second bound lands beneath it.
The old caption sets and is struck through.
Two evidence rows land underneath with the medians and the zero-day rates.

props.title: Two things the thirty days is not

bounds.label: not diligence
bounds.text: The lag cannot be shorter than the reporting calendar. Across 55 period ends the panel sees only 5 distinct days of the month, so a manager filing on the 30th cannot reflect a 31st repricing any sooner.

bounds.label: not first-to-last
bounds.text: Median to ALL holders is 90 days and the tail runs to 427, but that counts managers still carrying an old level — staleness, not propagation.

props.struckLabel: and a claim that came out
props.struck: the biggest events are the fastest
props.evidenceNote: 27 days against 30 is three days on 9 events, and the SMALLER ones reach the same period end more often — 12/28 against 3/9. The caption was replaced with counts that hold.
props.source: SOURCE: figdata_week8.json — propagation.stagger, propagation.caveat; the big/small split is computed at injection

beats.narration_text: Every one of those numbers runs behind a guard. Two hundred and ninety-four unpriced marks, and three hundred and one on a split-blocked series, are excluded before any statistic is computed. No unadjudicated split, no incomplete run. And the report says plainly what none of this shows. These are fund marks, not transactions.

shot.visual_intent: The subtraction is performed on screen, and the reel ends on its own limits rather than its findings.

show.event: The panel total sets, then the two exclusions subtract in sequence.

show.at: on 'no unadjudicated split, no incomplete run'
show.event: Three zero counters land as a row.
Three limits land beneath a rule, in the author's own words.

props.title: What was excluded before anything was counted

zeroes.label: statistics run over an incomplete run

notShown: These are fund marks, not transactions. Nobody traded at these prices.
A spread between two managers is not a disagreement about value — B05 shows why.
A lag is observability, not diligence — the reporting calendar sets the floor.
props.source: SOURCE: figdata_week8.json — guards{}; the measured population is derived, not asserted

beats.narration_text: Week eight on one page. Five thousand one hundred and seventy-eight marks measured, after the guards. Twenty-five percent of steps carried forward unchanged against a plan that expected thirty to forty, and it holds under every widening I tried. That headline runs from zero to forty-eight percent by company, so on its own it describes nobody. Managers pricing the same company on the same date usually hold different prices, and one opened window shows why. A new level reaches half its holders in a median of thirty days, which measures observability, not diligence. Next week, back to building.

show.event: The Claude artifact page opens — Measuring How Private Marks Move and Propagate, week 8.
Five findings stagger in, one per spoken clause.

props.artifactTitle: Measuring How Private Marks Move and Propagate — week 8
artifactLines: 5,178 marks measured — 5,479 less 301 on split-blocked series. 0 unadjudicated splits, 0 incomplete runs.

25.0% of 4,079 consecutive observations unchanged, against a plan expecting 30–40%. Widening “unchanged” to ±0.1% gives 26.3% and to ±1% gives 29.6% — all still under the band, so this is a result and not a threshold.
By company the same statistic runs 0.0% (Groq) to 48.5% (X.AI Corp). One panel-wide number describes none of them.

130 same-date groups, median spread 10.8%, 92 holding more than one price level. One opened window — Anthropic preferred, 8 managers, 11 marks — shows a round arriving rather than a disagreement about value.
37 levels adopted by 3+ managers: median 30 days to half, 15 on the same period end, slowest 92. Observability, not diligence — and the “biggest events are fastest” claim did not survive checking.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Take a statistic you report as a single number and split it by the most obvious dimension you have. Customer, region, product, whatever it is. Then ask whether the headline still describes anything. Mine ran from zero to forty-eight percent, which means the panel-wide figure was true of no company in it. A number that is true on average and wrong everywhere is worse than no number.

show.event: Composer returns, greeting reads 'Your turn.'
The suggested prompt types itself in as the narration reads it aloud, verbatim.
